clue.text: Hat giving protection in nursery

definitions.meaning: a close-fitting bell-shaped woman's hat of the 1920s
a glass or plastic cover set over young plants in a plant nursery or garden

explanation.surface: A sunhat keeps a child's head safe in the nursery.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a bell-shaped hat and the bell-shaped glass cover gardeners put over seedlings.

clue.text: Prior, Swift and Pope, for example

definitions.text: Prior, Swift and Pope, for example

parts.words: Prior, Swift and Pope, for example
parts.note: reads as three English poets (Matthew Prior, Jonathan Swift, Alexander Pope), but a prior and a pope are clerics, and Swift was a dean

explanation.surface: A list of three Augustan writers offered as examples of a type.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals steer you to literature; strip them and a prior and a pope are religious office-holders, while Swift was Dean of St Patrick's in Dublin.
explanation.definitionFit: Clergymen: a prior heads a priory, a pope heads the Catholic Church and Swift served as a cathedral dean.

clue.text: Survive in first?

parts.note: the saying 'first in, last out': whoever went in first comes ..., so outliving the others

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether getting in first is the way to come through.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'in first' against its opposite: the one who goes in first comes out last, and to come out last is to survive everyone else.
explanation.definitionFit: To survive others is to continue living longer than they do, to be the final one remaining.

clue.text: Overbearing as victim of hold-up?

definitions.meaning: bossy and arrogant, using power without regard for others
a robbery victim told 'hands up' stands with hands held high

explanation.surface: A bully is compared to someone caught in a robbery.
explanation.definitionFit: Domineering behaviour is called this; the same phrase literally pictures a victim with arms raised at gunpoint.

clue.text: Understood 13 beheaded in accordance with the law

indicators.note: having the head cut off means the first letter of the word from clue 13 is dropped

parts.note: the answer to 13 across, a trimming
licit means lawful, permitted by law

explanation.surface: Something tacitly understood is said to be lawful once the head is removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beheaded' strips G from GIMP, the answer to 13, leaving IMP.
explanation.definitionFit: Something implicit is grasped without being stated outright, so it is tacitly understood.

clue.text: Self-willed maiden creates a fluster

parts.note: M is the cricket scoring abbreviation for a maiden over

indicators.note: the letters of the phrase a fluster are made into something new, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A headstrong young woman stirs up confusion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'creates' rearranges A FLUSTER into ASTERFUL; a maiden in cricket is an over with no runs scored.
explanation.definitionFit: Masterful people impose their own wishes on others, so they are domineering and wilful.

clue.text: Idle head

explanation.surface: An idler is called an empty head.
explanation.definitionFit: To loaf is to laze; 'loaf' is also British slang for the head, from rhyming slang loaf of bread.

clue.text: Goldsmith joining small group in Irish capital

parts.note: a cell is a small unit of activists within a larger organisation

indicators.note: a capital letter is the first one, so the opening letter of the word Irish is taken

explanation.surface: A craftsman in gold joins a small circle in Dublin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irish capital' looks like Dublin, but 'capital' means the first letter of 'Irish', I. Benvenuto Cellini was a Renaissance Italian goldsmith and sculptor.
explanation.definitionFit: Benvenuto Cellini, the Florentine Renaissance artist, was famous as a goldsmith and sculptor.

clue.text: Fill pot

parts.note: read as instructions, the answer says put the word top upwards, which in a down clue gives pot

explanation.surface: An instruction to fill a cooking pot.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: take the answer as wordplay, TOP written UP (backwards, in a down light), and it spells 'pot'.
explanation.definitionFit: To fill a glass or tank again to the brim is to replenish it.

clue.text: This college sent down no odd characters, however

indicators.note: dropping the odd-numbered letters keeps only the even ones of the words sent down

explanation.surface: A college expels a student, though nobody strange is involved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no odd characters' means skip letters 1, 3, 5, 7 of 'sent down', keeping E, T, O, N. 'Sent down' wants to mean expelled from college, which fits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton is the famous English public school founded by Henry VI, formally Eton College.

clue.text: Nervously tense, like a rider when drunk

parts.note: a jockey who is up is mounted on the horse
tight is informal for drunk

explanation.surface: A jittery horseman who has been drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone uptight is anxious and on edge, unable to relax.

clue.text: Betray everyone in this boat

indicators.note: one word placed within another: everyone goes inside the word for betray

parts.note: to shop someone is British slang for informing on them to the police
all means everyone

explanation.surface: A traitor turns in everyone aboard a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts ALL inside SHOP. A shallop is a light open boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A shallop is a small light open boat, propelled by oars or sails.

clue.text: Ulster may depend on one

parts.note: the capital suggests Northern Ireland relying on someone, but an ulster is a long heavy overcoat that hangs from something in a wardrobe

explanation.surface: Northern Ireland relies on a single ally.
explanation.walkthrough: An ulster is a long loose overcoat with a cape; the capital U is only there because it opens the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Coats are hung on a shaped frame with a hook, so an overcoat literally hangs from one.

clue.text: Trimming a couple of army men

parts.note: a GI is an American soldier
an MP is a military policeman

explanation.surface: Tidying up a pair of soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: The two army men are a GI (US soldier) and an MP (military policeman).
explanation.definitionFit: Gimp is a twisted silk or cotton cord used as decorative edging on clothes and furniture.

clue.text: Time launch round day's end in part of Ireland

indicators.note: one word goes round another, so the launch timing encloses a letter

parts.note: a countdown times the seconds to a rocket launch

indicators.note: the end of the word day's is its final letter

explanation.surface: Counting the moments to a launch near the close of the day somewhere in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' puts COUNTDOWN around Y, the last letter of 'day's'. County Down is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: County Down is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland, on its east coast.

clue.text: Play in afternoon with new England opener in team

indicators.note: making something new of these letters means rearranging them
the opener of the word England is its first letter

explanation.surface: A cricket side brings in a new England opening batsman for an afternoon fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opener' gives E from England; 'new' rearranges E + IN + TEAM. The cricket surface hides the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A matinee is a theatre or cinema performance held in the afternoon.

clue.text: Absorbed what's writ large

definitions.meaning: a legal document copied out in large formal handwriting is said to be ...

explanation.surface: Being absorbed in something that is written in large letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An engrossed reader is rapt; a deed fair-copied in a large clerk's hand is also said to be engrossed.

clue.text: Half-baked pudding is hard

parts.note: a fool is a dessert of fruit purée folded into cream
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: An undercooked dessert turns out tough.
explanation.walkthrough: A fool is a British dessert of fruit (often gooseberry) folded into cream.
explanation.definitionFit: Half-baked ideas are silly and ill-thought-out, so they are senseless.

clue.text: Conceal spring that's narrow and rigid

parts.note: hide means conceal
a bound is a leap or spring

explanation.surface: Concealing a spring that is stiff and inflexible.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidebound person is set in their ways and unwilling to consider new ideas.

clue.text: Gets inside information in return for savings

indicators.note: coming back means the whole assembled string is read backwards
one word goes inside another: gets is placed within the word for information

parts.note: gen is British slang for information
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone receives insider tips in exchange for their savings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' puts GETS within GEN, making GGETSEN; 'in return' reverses it all. A nest egg is money saved up.
explanation.definitionFit: A nest egg is a sum of money put aside for the future.

clue.text: Half-prepared to make big strides in Cambridgeshire

definitions.meaning: someone with just one stilt strapped on is only halfway ready to walk on stilts
a village near Peterborough in Cambridgeshire, home of the cheese's name

explanation.surface: Someone half-ready to stride out across Cambridgeshire.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text had a stray gap mark; the page prints the clue whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Stilton is a village in Cambridgeshire, giving its name to the blue cheese; split, the word pictures one leg pole fitted.

clue.text: Boy holds sort of yarn or rope for fastening

indicators.note: one word holds another, so the boy encloses the rearranged letters

parts.note: lad means boy

indicators.note: a sort of something is a version of it, so the letters of yarn are rearranged

explanation.surface: A boy holding some kind of yarn or cord used for tying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges YARN into NYAR, which 'holds' puts inside LAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A lanyard is a short cord or line used on ships to secure things, or worn to hold a whistle or pass.

clue.text: Complaint porter intended to be heard

indicators.note: something to be heard is spoken, signalling words that sound like the answer

parts.note: porter is a dark beer, an ale; intended means meant

explanation.surface: A grumble that a hotel porter meant to make audible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be heard' says ALE MEANT (porter intended) is spoken aloud. Porter is a dark British beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint in the medical sense is an illness or disorder.

clue.text: Heartlessness, perhaps? Nothing in it

definitions.meaning: in bridge, holding no cards of one suit, such as no hearts

explanation.surface: Wondering whether being heartless means there is nothing inside.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, a hand with no cards at all in one suit has a void in it, so no hearts is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridge hand lacking one suit has a void there; and empty space with nothing in it is also called this.

clue.text: For example, a volume about partners

indicators.note: one word goes about another, so the volume surrounds the partners

parts.note: we, a pair of people together, as in bridge partners

explanation.surface: An example of a book volume concerning partnerships.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts WE inside VOL. 'For example, a' looks like the start of a sentence, but the letter A is the thing defined.
explanation.definitionFit: The letter A is one of the five letters a, e, i, o, u that stand for open sounds.

clue.text: Right group gets card early in week

parts.note: Monday is the first working day
a club is a playing card of the club suit

explanation.surface: A right-wing faction is dealt a card at the start of the week.
explanation.walkthrough: The Monday Club was a right-wing pressure group linked to the British Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: The Monday Club was a political pressure group on the right of the British Conservative Party.

clue.text: Fruit a number of Romans consumed

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500
ate means consumed

explanation.surface: Many Romans ate some fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: The date is the sweet fruit of the date palm.

clue.text: Man's place as PM once

definitions.meaning: a town on the west coast of the Isle of Man
Sir Robert ... was British Prime Minister in the nineteenth century

explanation.surface: A man's position described as a former Prime Minister's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is the Isle of Man, an island in the Irish Sea, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Peel is a town on the Isle of Man, and Robert Peel served as Prime Minister twice.

clue.text: Declines part of Arab

definitions.meaning: the ridge between a horse's shoulder blades, here on an Arab horse

explanation.surface: Something goes downhill in a part of the Arab world.
explanation.walkthrough: An Arab is a breed of horse, and the withers are the high point of its back.
explanation.definitionFit: Withering is shrivelling away; the withers are the ridge at the top of a horse's shoulders.

clue.text: Hear out novel writer

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters of the phrase hear out are given a new order

explanation.surface: An author asks us to listen to the whole of a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' rearranges HEAR OUT; it poses as the book a writer produces.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry David Thoreau was the American essayist who wrote Walden.

clue.text: She lets country boy away, finally

parts.note: land means country
lad means boy

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word away

explanation.surface: A woman lets a country lad leave in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She lets' looks like the start of a sentence, but it defines a woman who lets out rooms.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who rents out rooms or a house to tenants is the one who lets property.

clue.text: How do we stand one?

definitions.meaning: from the slogan '... we stand, divided we fall'

explanation.surface: Someone asks how we stand with one another.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying runs 'together we stand, divided we fall'; and people joined as one are combined.
